accuracy.evidence: Checked against the national curriculum in England, English Appendix 2 Year 6 (use of the colon to introduce a list and use of semi-colons within lists) and the Years 5–6 writing programme, and against the Oxford Guide to Style / New Hart's Rules and the Chicago Manual of Style 6.65 (a colon introducing a list follows a complete clause and should not separate a verb or preposition from its object or complement) and 6.60 (semicolons separate items in a series when items contain internal commas, including before the final conjunction). Every lab sentence was checked by hand: each lead-in judged complete/incomplete, each semicolon list rebuilt, every item count recounted.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented errors with list punctuation: a colon straight after a verb (We need:, are:, held:, were: in LEAD, FIX 1 and 3, prediction 1, challenge q1/q4, m2); a semicolon used to open a list (FIX 2, BUILD gap 0 feedback, m8); mixing commas and semicolons between items (FIX 4, p5, challenge q5); counting commas inside an item as extra items (COUNT 'too many' feedback, prediction 3, m4); turning internal commas into semicolons (SEMI wrong-tap feedback 'it is inside one item'); and using semicolons for simple lists (challenge q2, m9).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagcolsemi is built on the boundary between a lead-in and its list and between whole items: a complete-sentence test for the colon gap, a list shown with only commas where the learner taps just the commas that sit between whole items, item counting where semicolons settle ambiguity, a tap-the-wrong-mark check of colon/semicolon slips, and a drag of : ; , chips into blue gaps to build a list from scratch. flagambig (809) covers comma meaning and flaglist-style comma labs (370) cover simple lists; none treats colons or semicolons. lab_distinct gate under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The rule is discovered by the test, not stated first: choosing Add a colon after We need returns 'need must run straight on to what we need'; tapping the comma inside Paris, France returns 'it is inside one item'; tapping 5 for 'Sam, my cousin; Ella; and Jo' says a comma inside an item does not start a new one; dragging ; into the first gap says a semicolon cannot open a list; dragging , between items with commas says it hides where one item ends.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with a tempting wrong option the task disproves: 'yes, a list follows' for We need ▢ (LEAD 2 is No colon), 'commas are fine here' for Paris, France, Rome, Italy and Oslo, Norway (SEMI 1 shows the reader cannot tell items apart until semicolons go in), and '4' people for 'Sam, my cousin, Ella and Jo' (COUNT 1 and 2 show the same names giving 3 or 4 depending on semicolons). A.reveal names the locked-in pick at the end of each task.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with twelve wrong-answer messages naming the slip: Bring is not a complete sentence, a list opens with a colon not a semicolon, simple items only need commas (twice), commas inside an item do not add people, count the items between semicolons, a colon after are or need cuts the verb from its list, between items use commas or semicolons, the comma inside Rome, Italy stays, keep semicolons going once started, semicolons are for clarity not length, and a colon opens the list.

readability.evidence: learn/readability.py: kid FK grade 3.5 (family limit 5.0), adult 9.9 (limit 10.0). Kid paragraphs give one example each (You will need three things: a torch, a map and a drink; We need: eggs and milk is a slip; Paris, France; Rome, Italy). Canvas sentences are under 15 words, and feedback is one or two short sentences. Lab trimmed under the 20 KB pre-commit limit by shortening why-text, not removing feedback.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs cover what a colon looks like and when it opens a list, the no-colon-after-a-verb rule, semicolons for items with commas, and counting; adult text gives the Year 6 Appendix 2 statement, the complete-sentence test, the semicolon-before-and convention, the named mistakes and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler and the explanation is under 12% similar to every other lesson, including 370 commas in lists and 809 commas to avoid ambiguity.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px Android screenshots in light and dark for all six steps and wrong-answer states (No colon tapped for a complete lead-in, the comma inside Oslo, Norway tapped, 5 tapped for a 3-person list, the full stop tapped as wrong, a comma dragged into the colon gap). Mark chips are at least 40 px tall with extra padding for single characters; the full stop now joins the last word; the gap ring switches to light blue on dark after it was too faint. Walkthrough passed on iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: Every tap and drag has a button under the canvas: Add a colon / No colon (labelled with the lead-in), one button per tappable comma (', after Paris', labelled 'Make the comma after Paris a semicolon'), the item counts, one button per mark in the fix sentence, and : ; , buttons that fill the next gap (labelled 'Put a colon in the next gap'). The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action, challenge feedback is a role=status live region, warnings switch to #fda4af on dark, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
